title: Gold on the Harmandir
hook: he covers the Harmandir in gilded copper and marble, and it becomes the Golden Temple

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Sarkar-e-Khalsa, a kingdom named for the Khalsa, with coins in the Gurus' names; your line was the khalsa's rule. Today, gold.

Early morning at Amritsar. Mist on the water, kirtan carrying across the pool, and in the middle of it all a building that catches the first light and throws it back gold. People photograph that glow from every side of the pool. But the building wasn't always gold. This path has watched it rise, be desecrated, be blown up, and be rebuilt by the misls with plain hands and hard work. Today, someone covers it in light.
screen: `MIST ON THE POOL AT DAWN.` → `A BUILDING THAT GLOWS.` → `IT WASN'T ALWAYS GOLD.`

segments.voice: Begin with what it already was: the Harmandir Sahib, also called Darbar Sahib, the court of the Lord. Guru Arjan built it in the middle of the pool at Amritsar and placed the scripture inside. Tradition loves one detail: doors on every side, open to anyone from any direction. Then the hard years, when it was attacked and destroyed more than once, and the misls rebuilt it. Now Ranjit Singh. With a kingdom behind him, he gave the Harmandir its gold. The upper part was covered with copper plates, and the copper was gilded, given a skin of gold. The lower walls were faced with marble, inlaid with stones and flower patterns. Craftsmen worked on it a long time, and slowly the building Sikhs called the Harmandir became the one the world calls the Golden Temple. Here's what matters. He didn't build a temple of his own. He took the Gurus' house, built by Guru Arjan and rebuilt by ordinary Sikhs, and gilded it. Once more, the king's wealth pointed past the king. In the Guru Granth Sahib, a hymn of Guru Arjan says that God himself stood up to finish the work of the saints; tradition links it to the finishing of the pool, and it is still sung when a piece of work is finished. The gold says the same thing in metal: this work is the Guru's, and the best there is belongs here.
screen: `DOORS ON EVERY SIDE, OPEN TO ALL.` · `DESTROYED, THEN REBUILT.` · `COPPER, GOLD AND MARBLE.` · `THE GURUS' HOUSE, NOT HIS.` · then, large: `GOLD FOR THE GURU.`

segments.voice: If you can, pick up one small thing near you that you love but have let go dull, a ring, a frame, a cup, and polish it slowly with a cloth or your sleeve, as if it belonged to someone you honor; if there's nothing to hand, polish it in your mind. Watch the shine come back and notice your hands while they work, with Waheguru on each breath out if you pray.
Harmandir, the house Guru Arjan built at Amritsar, given gilded copper above and marble below by Ranjit Singh. Today's word.
Your line: gold for the guru. The Gurus' house, not his. Day nine hundred eleven.

chat.says: Did Ranjit Singh build the Golden Temple?
options: No; Guru Arjan built it. Ranjit Singh gave it gilded copper above and marble below.
Yes; he built it new in gold, to stand as the jewel of his own kingdom.
No; the British gilded it later, as a gift after the treaty on the Sutlej.
chat.meaning: Guru Arjan built the Harmandir and the misls rebuilt it; Ranjit Singh gilded the Gurus' house rather than build his own.

notes: Editor pass: replaced 'burn' with 'be desecrated'; cut the time claims 'hard century' and 'for weeks'; softened 'no misl chief could afford'; the link between the Ang 783 hymn and the pool is now framed as tradition.
Claims rule: no counts or dates spoken; the doors are described as on every side rather than counted.
Gilded copper plates on the upper structure and marble on the lower walls under Ranjit Singh: standard account; confirm. 'Craftsmen worked on it a long time' kept vague.
Darbar Sahib glossed as 'the court of the Lord': confirm.
Doors on every side, open to all: common tradition; confirm phrasing.

Ang 783, Suhi M5, 'santa ke kaaraj aap khaloia' paraphrased as God standing up to finish the work of the saints, and said to be sung at the completion of a task: confirm Ang, paraphrase and practice claim.

Audit: myth 'he put his own name over the door' (false) was wrong; an inscription at the entrance does name Maharaja Ranjit Singh, as the Guru's servant granted the seva. Myth and voice now say only that he built no new temple of his own. Cut the unsourced 'something no misl chief had given it' and softened the singing claim.
